title: Actaeon
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Actaeon, Cadmus' grandson, calls off the hunt at noon and strays into the valley of Gargaphie, where Diana is bathing; she has no weapon to hand but the water she is being bathed in, and she flings it in his face. He leaves the grove a stag, with his own mind left untouched inside the animal, and his own hounds — named one by one in a long catalogue — run him down. Ovid states in his second sentence that what he finds in Actaeon is fortune's fault and not a crime, and the tale's last line hands the question of Diana's anger over to rumour.

sentences.t:
Prima nepos inter tot res tibi, Cadme, secundas
causa fuit luctus, alienaque cornua fronti
addita, vosque canes satiatae sanguine erili.
sentences.l: The first cause of grief, amid so many favourable things for you, Cadmus, was your grandson — and horns belonging to another, added to his forehead, and you, hounds, glutted with your master's blood.
sentences.i: Amid so much that went well for you, Cadmus, the first cause of grief was your grandson — and the antlers that were not his, set on his forehead, and you, hounds, gorged on your master's blood.
sentences.n: Apostrophe: Ovid breaks off from narrating to address Cadmus directly (tibi, Cadme), then the dogs (vosque canes). He does it constantly, and it is a way of putting the reader inside the grief rather than in front of it. The tale is told backwards from its end before it begins: we are given the antlers and the blood first. nepos = grandson; Actaeon is the son of Cadmus' daughter Autonoe.

sentences.t:
At bene si quaeras, fortunae crimen in illo,
non scelus invenies: quod enim scelus error habebat?
sentences.l: But if you should ask rightly, you will find in him the charge of fortune, not a crime: for what crime did a straying hold?
sentences.i: But ask properly, and what you will find laid against him is fortune's charge, not a crime: what crime was there in going astray?
sentences.n: The whole case for the defence, laid down before the evidence. crimen is the charge brought, scelus the wrong actually done; error is a wandering off — and Actaeon will literally wander, non certis passibus, into the grove at 175–176. si quaeras… invenies is a condition with one foot in each mood — a subjunctive 'were one to ask' answered by a flat future 'you will find'; the second person is the indefinite one, addressed to anybody at all. The last line of the tale will reopen the question.

sentences.t: Mons erat infectus variarum caede ferarum;
sentences.l: There was a mountain stained with the slaughter of wild beasts of every kind;
sentences.i: There was a mountain steeped in the slaughter of every kind of wild beast;
sentences.n: infectus is 'dyed, stained' — the mountain is coloured with blood. The same verb comes back at 183 of clouds stained by the sun, and of Diana's blush. The tale opens on killing that nobody calls a crime.

sentences.t:
iamque dies medius rerum contraxerat umbras
et sol ex aequo meta distabat utraque,
cum iuvenis placido per devia lustra vagantes
participes operum compellat Hyantius ore:
sentences.l: and now the middle of the day had drawn in the shadows of things, and the sun stood equally distant from each turning-post, when the young man addresses, with calm voice, his partners in the work as they wander through the trackless coverts — the Hyantian:
sentences.i: and now noon had pulled in every shadow and the sun hung midway between its two turning-posts, when the young Boeotian called in a quiet voice to his fellow-huntsmen as they ranged the trackless coverts:
sentences.n: meta is the turning-post at each end of a Roman racecourse: the sun's day is a chariot race, and at noon it is equidistant from both ends. The inverted cum-clause ('when suddenly…') carries the main event of the sentence. Hyantius = 'the Hyantian', i.e. Boeotian, from the old people of that land — Ovid will go ninety lines without saying Actaeon's name, and here he strands the epithet at the end of the line where the name should be.

sentences.t:
“Lina madent, comites, ferrumque cruore ferarum,
fortunamque dies habuit satis.
sentences.l: 'The nets are soaked, comrades, and the iron too, with the blood of wild beasts, and the day has had good fortune enough.
sentences.i: 'Our nets are soaked, friends, and our steel with them, in the beasts' blood, and the day has had luck enough.
sentences.n: One ablative, cruore ferarum, does duty for both subjects: nets and iron alike are soaked with it. ferrum, 'the iron', is metonymy for the hunting spears — Latin verse names weapons by their metal. satis is adverbial with habuit — fortunam is the object, and the day has had good luck 'enough'; some editions print fortunaeque instead, making satis a noun with a partitive genitive, 'enough of luck', with no change of sense.

sentences.l: 'When another Dawn, borne in on saffron wheels, shall bring the light back, we shall take up again the work we set ourselves;
sentences.i: 'When tomorrow's Dawn rides in on her saffron wheels and brings the light back, we take up the task again;
sentences.n: cum is postponed to third word inside its own clause — ordinary in verse, and a habit worth expecting: the conjunction is often not where an English reader looks for it. Aurora drives a chariot, so invecta is a passive participle in a middle sense, 'having ridden herself in'. Latin keeps the future strictly (reducet, repetemus) where English slides into the present.

sentences.t:
nunc Phoebus utraque
distat idem terra finditque vaporibus arva.
sentences.l: 'now Phoebus stands off, one and the same distance, from each land, and splits the fields with his steaming heat.
sentences.i: 'now the sun is equally far from either land and cracks the fields open with heat.
sentences.n: Magnus prints terra ('from each land', i.e. east and west); other editions print meta, 'from each turning-post', which puts the narrator's racecourse image of 145 back into Actaeon's own mouth — a real difference in what the line does. idem is nominative masculine agreeing with Phoebus but working adverbially, 'at the same distance alike'. findit is the verb for ground gaping in drought.

sentences.t: Sistite opus praesens nodosaque tollite lina.”
sentences.l: 'Halt the work in hand and take up the knotted nets.'
sentences.i: 'Break off the work in hand and lift the knotted nets.'
sentences.n: tollite is 'take up' in the sense of gathering in and packing away, not raising for use — the day's hunting is over. The knots are the nets' working parts; Ovid names them because he has just called the nets soaked.

sentences.t: Iussa viri faciunt intermittuntque laborem.
sentences.l: They do the man's orders and break off their labour.
sentences.i: They do as he orders and leave the work off.
sentences.n: iussa is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, 'the things ordered' — Latin does this constantly and English has to supply a noun. One flat line of obedience, and the trap is set: the hunt stops early, which is the only thing Actaeon actually does.

sentences.t:
Vallis erat piceis et acuta densa cupressu,
nomine Gargaphie, succinctae sacra Dianae.
sentences.l: There was a valley thick with pitch-pines and sharp cypress, Gargaphie by name, sacred to girt-up Diana.
sentences.i: There was a valley dense with pitch-pine and pointed cypress, Gargaphie by name, sacred to Diana of the tucked-up robe.
sentences.n: succincta — with the tunic gathered short at the waist for running — is Diana's standing description as huntress, and it is the exact opposite of how she will be seen twenty lines later. acuta of the cypress means its tapering shape. Gargaphie is a real valley in Boeotia; cupressu is a collective singular — one word for the whole stand of cypress — while piceis beside it is a plain ablative plural, the two constructions sitting side by side under the one adjective densa.

sentences.t:
Cuius in extremo est antrum nemorale recessu,
arte laboratum nulla: simulaverat artem
ingenio natura suo; nam pumice vivo
et levibus tofis nativum duxerat arcum.
sentences.l: In its farthest recess there is a wooded cave, worked by no art: nature had counterfeited art with her own genius; for out of living pumice and light tufa she had drawn a native arch.
sentences.i: Deep in its farthest recess lies a cave among the trees, made by no craft: nature had imitated art out of her own talent, drawing a natural vault from living pumice and light tufa.
sentences.n: cuius opens the sentence as a connecting relative — 'and of it', not a question; Latin joins sentences this way where English starts a new one. Present est sits inside past narrative: the cave is still there. The art-versus-nature conceit is a Roman commonplace with a joke inside it — wealthy Romans built artificial grottoes to look like this one. pumex vivus is rock still in place, unquarried, and duxerat arcum is the builder's phrase for turning a vault. levibus is ambiguous without macrons — levis 'light' or lēvis 'smooth' — and either reads well beside pumice vivo; Lectorium prints 'light' without claiming to have settled it.

sentences.t:
Fons sonat a dextra, tenui perlucidus unda,
margine gramineo patulos succinctus hiatus.
sentences.l: A spring sounds on the right, transparent with its thin water, girt as to its wide-open mouths with a grassy margin.
sentences.i: On the right a spring sounds, clear through its shallow water, its broad basin girdled with a rim of grass.
sentences.n: hiatus is accusative plural after the passive participle succinctus — the Greek accusative of respect, 'girt as to its gaping mouths'. Ovid uses it constantly; the giveaway is a stray accusative with no verb to govern it. Note that the spring is succinctus with the same word used of Diana at 156: the water is dressed as she is. (Magnus prints succinctus; some editions read incinctus, which loses the echo of 156.)

sentences.t:
Hic dea silvarum venatu fessa solebat
virgineos artus liquido perfundere rore.
sentences.l: Here the goddess of the woods, tired out with hunting, used to drench her maiden limbs in the clear dew.
sentences.i: Here the goddess of the woods, worn out with hunting, would bathe her maiden limbs in the clear water.
sentences.n: solebat, imperfect of habit: the ambush is built out of a routine. ros is properly dew, extended in verse to any clear running water. virgineos is the word the whole disaster turns on — not that she is naked, but that she is a virgin goddess and is seen.

sentences.t:
Quo postquam subiit, nympharum tradidit uni
armigerae iaculum pharetramque arcusque retentos;
sentences.l: After she had come in there, she handed to one of the nymphs, her armour-bearer, her javelin and quiver and unstrung bows;
sentences.i: Once inside, she handed her javelin, her quiver and her unstrung bow to one of the nymphs, her armour-bearer;
sentences.n: quo is a connecting relative adverb, 'to which place'. arcus is a fourth-declension accusative plural — the poetic plural for her one bow, which is why the idiomatic layer prints a singular — and retentos is from retendere, 'to unbend a bow' — the bow is slack because the hunting is done. (Some take it instead from retinere, 'held back for her'.) armigera, 'armour-bearer', is a soldier's word: her household is run like a war-band, and she has just disarmed.

sentences.t:
altera depositae subiecit bracchia pallae,
vincla duae pedibus demunt;
sentences.l: another put her arms under the laid-aside robe, two take the bindings from her feet;
sentences.i: another held her arms out under the robe as it came off, two unfasten her sandals;
sentences.n: depositae pallae is dative with subiecit, and the participle runs slightly ahead of events — the arms go under the robe as it is being put off. Watch the tenses: perfect subiecit stands beside present demunt in the same sentence. Ovid alternates perfect and historic present all through this tale, slowing to record and then speeding to watch.

sentences.t:
nam doctior illis
Ismenis Crocale sparsos per colla capillos
conligit in nodum, quamvis erat ipsa solutis.
sentences.l: for more skilled than they, Ismenian Crocale gathers the hair scattered over her neck into a knot, although she herself was with hers loose.
sentences.i: for Ismenian Crocale, defter than the rest, gathers into a knot the hair spilling down Diana's neck — though her own she wore loose.
sentences.n: Ismenis is a Greek feminine form in -is from Ismenus, the Boeotian river-god — either 'Ismenian' or 'daughter of Ismenus', and Lectorium prints the adjective without settling it; Ovid keeps Greek names in Greek shapes throughout this tale. quamvis normally takes the subjunctive, but erat here is indicative, a licence Ovid allows himself in verse: read it as a flat statement of fact, 'though her own hair actually was loose'. solutis is an ablative with capillis simply left out — the reader supplies the noun from the previous clause. The last four words are a small joke: the hairdresser's own hair is down.

sentences.t:
Excipiunt laticem Nepheleque Hyaleque Rhanisque
et Psecas et Phiale funduntque capacibus urnis.
sentences.l: Nephele and Hyale and Rhanis and Psecas and Phiale catch the water and pour it from capacious urns.
sentences.i: Nephele and Hyale and Rhanis, Psecas and Phiale catch the water and pour it out from their broad urns.
sentences.n: Every name is a water-word in Greek: Nephele 'cloud', Hyale 'crystal', Rhanis 'raindrop', Psecas 'drizzle', Phiale 'bowl'. Ovid names creatures after what they are and then makes them do it — a habit that is about to be run at full length on the hounds. The piled -que…-que…et…et keeps the pouring going without a pause.

sentences.t:
Dumque ibi perluitur solita Titania lympha,
ecce nepos Cadmi dilata parte laborum
per nemus ignotum non certis passibus errans
pervenit in lucum:
sentences.l: And while the Titan's granddaughter is being bathed there in her accustomed water, behold, Cadmus' grandson, his share of the labours put off, wandering with steps not sure through an unknown wood, arrives at the grove:
sentences.i: And while the Titan's granddaughter is bathing there in her usual pool — look: Cadmus' grandson, his share of the day's work laid aside, straying with unsure steps through a wood he did not know, comes out into the grove:
sentences.n: dilata parte laborum is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with X done' phrase where English wants a whole clause ('now that he had put off…'). Latin uses it everywhere; expect it. Titania is 'descendant of the Titans': Diana, through her mother Latona. perluitur is passive in form but middle in sense, 'bathes herself'. non certis passibus and errans are the poem's own word error from 142, made literal.

sentences.t: sic illum fata ferebant.
sentences.l: so were the fates carrying him.
sentences.i: so his destiny was carrying him along.
sentences.n: Four words, and the verdict of 141–142 confirmed by the narrator: the imperfect ferebant makes it something being done to him while it happens, not something he does.

sentences.t:
Qui simul intravit rorantia fontibus antra,
sicut erant, viso nudae sua pectora nymphae
percussere viro, subitisque ululatibus omne
implevere nemus
sentences.l: And as soon as he entered the caves dripping with springs, just as they were, the nymphs, naked, at the sight of the man beat their own breasts and filled the whole wood with sudden shrieks,
sentences.i: The moment he stepped into the spring-wet cave, the nymphs — naked, exactly as they were — beat their breasts at the sight of the man and filled the whole wood with sudden screaming,
sentences.n: Qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative: 'and he'. viso… viro is another ablative absolute, 'the man having been seen'. percussere is percusserunt: the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere, which Ovid prefers in verse for the metre — implevere and texere follow immediately, and videre at 206 is the same form. sicut erant means just as they were — that is, unclothed.

sentences.t:
circumfusaeque Dianam
corporibus texere suis;
sentences.l: and, poured round about, they covered Diana with their own bodies;
sentences.i: and, crowding round her, screened Diana with their bodies;
sentences.n: circumfusae is again a passive participle doing middle work: 'having poured themselves around'. texere here is texerunt from tego, 'cover' — not the verb 'weave', which looks identical in the infinitive. The nymphs make a wall of bodies, which is the wrong defence against being looked at.

sentences.t:
tamen altior illis
ipsa dea est colloque tenus supereminet omnes.
sentences.l: yet the goddess herself is taller than they, and as far as the neck she overtops them all.
sentences.i: but the goddess herself stands taller than they, and from the neck up rises above them all.
sentences.n: collo tenus: tenus is a postposition, following the ablative it governs — 'as far as the neck'. altior illis is an ablative of comparison, 'taller than they', without quam. The detail is not decoration: her head and shoulders are above the screen, so she is seen, and the whole tale follows from those few inches.

sentences.t:
Qui color infectis adversi solis ab ictu
nubibus esse solet aut purpureae aurorae,
is fuit in vultu visae sine veste Dianae.
sentences.l: What colour clouds stained by the stroke of the facing sun are wont to have, or crimson dawn, that was in the face of Diana, seen without her clothing.
sentences.i: The colour that clouds take when the low sun strikes them full, or the colour of a crimson dawn — that was in Diana's face, seen without her robe.
sentences.n: Latin regularly puts the relative clause first and answers it with a demonstrative (qui color… is fuit) where English puts the main clause first; unpicking that order is half of reading Ovid. infectis picks up infectus from 143, the mountain stained with blood: the same verb now colours a blush. adversi solis is the sun facing the clouds, i.e. low and level. nubibus and purpureae aurorae are datives of possession with esse — 'the colour that is wont to belong to clouds… or to crimson dawn' — which is what accounts for the form aurorae; English turns them into the subject of 'have'.

sentences.t:
Quae quamquam comitum turba est stipata suarum,
in latus obliquum tamen adstitit oraque retro
flexit,
sentences.l: And she, although she was hemmed in by the crowd of her companions, nevertheless stood turned side-on and bent her face back,
sentences.i: And though she stood packed round by her crowd of attendants, she still turned side-on and twisted her face away,
sentences.n: Quae is again a connecting relative, 'and she'. quamquam takes the indicative, here the perfect est stipata — it concedes a fact, unlike a conditional concession. in latus obliquum adstitit is a body turning away by reflex, not a pose: she is a goddess and she is embarrassed, and the reflex takes precedence over the revenge by exactly one line.

sentences.t:
et ut vellet promptas habuisse sagittas,
quas habuit sic hausit aquas vultumque virilem
perfudit,
sentences.l: and, as she would have wished to have had her arrows ready to hand, so she drew up the waters which she did have and drenched the man's face,
sentences.i: and, just as she would have wished for her arrows ready to hand, so she caught up the one thing she did have — the water — and flung it over the man's face,
sentences.n: ut… sic is a correlative pair: 'as she would have wished for arrows, so she took up what she had'. The sic is what decides it — read ut as concessive ('granted that she wished') and sic is left with nothing to answer. habuisse is a perfect infinitive because the wish is for a state that is already past saving. The relative clause swallows its own antecedent — quas habuit… aquas, 'the waters which she had' — a word order Latin allows and English cannot. virilem carries the whole offence: it is a man's face, and that is all he has done.

sentences.t:
spargensque comas ultricibus undis
addidit haec cladis praenuntia verba futurae:
sentences.l: and sprinkling his hair with the avenging water she added these words, forerunners of the disaster to come:
sentences.i: and, scattering the avenging water over his hair, she added these words, heralds of the ruin to come:
sentences.n: praenuntia is a neuter plural in apposition to verba, and cladis… futurae is split wide around it, so that the coming disaster is wrapped around the words that announce it — Ovid separates a noun from its adjective for exactly this kind of effect. ultricibus does the work before the curse is spoken: the water is already the weapon.

sentences.t:
“Nunc tibi me posito visam velamine narres,
si poteris narrare, licet.”
sentences.l: 'Now you may tell that I was seen with my covering laid aside — if you shall be able to tell.'
sentences.i: 'Now you have my leave to tell that I was seen with my covering laid off — if you can still tell anything.'
sentences.n: The taunt is built out of its grammar. licet, 'it is permitted to you', takes narres as a bare subjunctive with no ut — the permission is real, and it is worthless. posito velamine is an ablative absolute, 'with the covering laid aside'. Then si poteris narrare is an open future condition in the plain indicative, about an outcome she has already decided: she is granting him the one thing she is in the act of taking away, and the future tense is the joke.

sentences.t:
Nec plura minata
dat sparso capiti vivacis cornua cervi,
dat spatium collo summasque cacuminat aures,
sentences.l: Having threatened nothing further, she gives to the sprinkled head the horns of a long-lived stag, gives length to the neck and brings the tips of the ears to a point,
sentences.i: With no further threat she sets on the drenched head the antlers of a long-lived stag, draws the neck out long, tapers the ear-tips to a point,
sentences.n: minata is a deponent participle: 'having threatened', active in sense though passive in form. The transformation replaces the speech — she stops talking and starts working. vivax, 'long-lived', is a cruelty: stags were proverbially long-lived, so she is handing him a long life in the wrong body. The repeated dat… dat and the present tense keep us watching it happen part by part; cacuminat, 'brings to a peak', is a rare verb Ovid may have coined.

sentences.t:
cum pedibusque manus, cum longis bracchia mutat
cruribus et velat maculoso vellere corpus.
sentences.l: and exchanges his hands for feet, his arms for long shanks, and clothes his body in a dappled hide.
sentences.i: and gives him feet in place of hands, long shanks in place of arms, and covers his body with a dappled hide.
sentences.n: mutat A cum B is 'exchange A for B', with the ablative naming what is received — so the doubled cum… cum… pairs each human limb with the animal thing that replaces it. vellus is properly a fleece; here the deer's coat. The arms go last of the limbs, and the loss of them will matter at 240–241.

sentences.t:
Additus et pavor est. Fugit Autonoeius heros
et se tam celerem cursu miratur in ipso.
sentences.l: Fear too was added. The Autonoëan hero flees, and in the very running wonders that he is so swift.
sentences.i: Terror was added too. Autonoe's son runs, and marvels in mid-flight at his own speed.
sentences.n: et here is 'also' (= etiam), postponed after the participle. Autonoeius is an adjective built from his mother's name — Ovid still will not say 'Actaeon', and the periphrases are piling up. heros keeps its Greek nominative. The last thing given him is the deer's instinct, and it starts working before he knows what he is.

sentences.t:
Ut vero vultus et cornua vidit in unda,
“me miserum!” dicturus erat: vox nulla secuta est.
sentences.l: But when he saw his face and horns in the water, 'wretched me!' he was about to say: no voice followed.
sentences.i: But when he saw his face and antlers in the water, 'Oh, wretch that I am!' he was going to say — no voice came.
sentences.n: me miserum is an accusative of exclamation, a fixed Latin cry with no verb; English has to add one. dicturus erat is a future participle with erat, 'was on the point of saying' — the words are fully formed and never become sound. He learns what he is from a reflection in water — the same element that was thrown at him a few lines before.

sentences.t:
Ingemuit: vox illa fuit, lacrimaeque per ora
non sua fluxerunt; mens tantum pristina mansit.
sentences.l: He groaned: that was his voice; and tears flowed down a face not his own; only his former mind remained.
sentences.i: He groaned — that was his voice now — and tears ran down a face that was not his; only the mind he had before was left.
sentences.n: vox illa fuit is three words that do the work of a paragraph: the groan is not a failed attempt at speech, it is the voice he now has. ora is a neuter plural used for a single face, standard in verse. mens pristina mansit is the hinge of the whole tale — the human mind is left inside the animal, which is why what follows is torture and not hunting; it also qualifies the pavor of 198, which turns out to be a body's reflex and not a change of mind.

sentences.t:
Quid faciat? repetatne domum et regalia tecta
an lateat silvis? pudor hoc, timor impedit illud.
sentences.l: What is he to do? Is he to make for home and the royal roof, or to lie hidden in the woods? Shame prevents this, fear that.
sentences.i: What is he to do? Make for home and the royal halls, or hide in the woods? Shame blocks the one, fear the other.
sentences.n: faciat, repetat, lateat are deliberative subjunctives — 'am I to…?' — reported in the third person, so we are inside his head without a word of speech. Which fear and which shame is genuinely unsettled: strictly hoc points to the nearer item (hiding) and illud to the further (going home), but readers have long reversed them, since shame at his shape fits the journey home. The Latin will support either, and Lectorium leaves it open.

sentences.t: Dum dubitat, videre canes.
sentences.l: While he hesitates, the hounds saw him.
sentences.i: While he is still hesitating, the hounds have seen him.
sentences.n: videre is viderunt, the poetic third-plural perfect again — and the sentence ends on canes, the verb thrown in front of its own subject so that the dogs arrive last, like a trap closing. The present dubitat against the perfect videre says his hesitation is still going on when the decision is taken out of his hands.

sentences.t:
Primumque Melampus
Ichnobatesque sagax latratu signa dedere,
Gnosius Ichnobates, Spartana gente Melampus.
sentences.l: And first Melampus and keen-nosed Ichnobates gave the signal by baying — Ichnobates of Gnosus, Melampus of Spartan stock.
sentences.i: First Melampus and sharp-nosed Ichnobates gave the signal with their baying — Ichnobates a Cretan, Melampus of Spartan breed.
sentences.n: The catalogue of hounds that begins here is a set-piece, and the joke running through it is that the names mean things: Melampus is 'Blackfoot', Ichnobates 'Track-treader', and so on for thirty-odd dogs. Lectorium leaves them untranslated in the Latin, as names, and glosses the sense in these notes rather than in the text — the Latin reader hears both at once, which is the effect Ovid wants. Gnosus (Cnossos) is in Crete: Cretan and Spartan were the two prestige hunting breeds, and Ovid gives the pack a pedigree before he gives it teeth. dedere = dederunt.

sentences.t:
Inde ruunt alii rapida velocius aura,
Pamphagus et Dorceus et Oribasus, Arcades omnes,
Nebrophonusque valens et trux cum Laelape Theron
et pedibus Pterelas et naribus utilis Agre,
sentences.l: Then the rest rush on, more swiftly than a racing wind — Pamphagus and Dorceus and Oribasus, Arcadians all, and strong Nebrophonus and savage Theron with Laelaps, and Pterelas, useful as to his feet, and Agre as to her nose,
sentences.i: Then the rest come on faster than a racing wind: Pamphagus, Dorceus, Oribasus — Arcadians every one — powerful Nebrophonus, savage Theron alongside Laelaps, Pterelas prized for his feet and Agre for her nose,
sentences.n: The names again say what the dogs are: Pamphagus 'Eat-all', Dorceus 'Gazelle', Oribasus 'Mountain-ranger', Nebrophonus 'Fawn-killer', Theron 'Hunter', Laelaps 'Squall', Pterelas 'Winged', Agre 'Chase'. pedibus and naribus are ablatives of respect with utilis, 'good as regards feet, as regards nostrils'. velocius aura is a comparative adverb with a plain ablative of comparison. Arcadia is the third of the famous hunting stocks, after Crete and Sparta.

sentences.t:
Hylaeusque ferox, nuper percussus ab apro,
deque lupo concepta Nape, pecudesque secuta
Poemenis et natis comitata Harpyia duobus,
sentences.l: and fierce Hylaeus, lately gashed by a boar, and Nape, conceived from a wolf, and Poemenis, who had followed flocks, and Harpyia, attended by two of her own young,
sentences.i: fierce Hylaeus, gored by a boar not long since; Nape, got by a wolf; Poemenis, who used to follow the flocks; Harpyia with two of her pups at heel,
sentences.n: Hylaeus 'Woodsman', Nape 'Glen', Poemenis 'Shepherdess' (and she is duly an ex-sheepdog), Harpyia 'Snatcher'. secuta is a deponent perfect participle in its normal active sense, 'having followed the flocks'; comitata beside it is the same kind of form used passively — 'accompanied by two young', with natis duobus an ablative and not its object — which comitor does regularly. What Ovid is doing here is giving the dogs biographies — an old wound, a wolf for a father, a former job, a litter — so that the pack stops being a weapon and becomes a household, which is what makes the end of the tale unbearable.

sentences.t:
et substricta gerens Sicyonius ilia Ladon,
et Dromas et Canache Sticteque et Tigris et Alce
et niveis Leucon et villis Asbolus atris
sentences.l: and Sicyonian Ladon, carrying his flanks drawn in, and Dromas and Canache and Sticte and Tigris and Alce, and Leucon with snowy coat and Asbolus with black,
sentences.i: Ladon of Sicyon, tucked up in the flank; Dromas, Canache, Sticte, Tigris, Alce; Leucon with his snow-white shag and Asbolus with his black,
sentences.n: The last line is a single interlocked phrase: niveis and atris both belong to the one noun villis, 'shaggy hairs', with one dog set beside each adjective, so the white dog and the black dog are woven into the same words. substricta ilia are the tucked-up loins of a greyhound. Names: Ladon (an Arcadian river), Dromas 'Runner', Canache 'Clang', Sticte 'Spot', Tigris 'Tiger', Alce 'Strength', Leucon 'Whitey', Asbolus 'Soot'.

sentences.t:
praevalidusque Lacon et cursu fortis Aello
et Thous et Cyprio velox cum fratre Lycisce,
sentences.l: and hugely strong Lacon and Aello, strong in running, and Thous and swift Lycisce with her Cyprian brother,
sentences.i: Lacon of enormous strength; Aello, strong on the run; Thous; and quick Lycisce with her Cyprian brother,
sentences.n: Lacon is simply 'the Spartan', Aello 'Storm-blast' (it is also the name of a Harpy), Thous 'Swift', Lycisce 'Wolf-bitch' — a half-wolf cross, like Nape at 214. The brother is the only member of the pack not given a name: he gets a birthplace instead, Cyprus being another noted source of hunting dogs.

sentences.t:
et nigram medio frontem distinctus ab albo
Harpalos, et Melaneus hirsutaque corpore Lachne,
sentences.l: and Harpalos, marked as to his black forehead with white in the middle, and Melaneus and Lachne, shaggy in body,
sentences.i: Harpalos, his black forehead split down the middle by a blaze of white; Melaneus; shaggy-bodied Lachne;
sentences.n: nigram… frontem is an accusative of respect after the passive participle distinctus — 'marked as regards his black forehead' — the Greek construction flagged at 162, and here impossible to mistake for anything else, since distinctus cannot take an object. Harpalos keeps its Greek -os nominative. The names: Harpalos 'Grabber', Melaneus 'Blackie', Lachne 'Fleece' — and Lachne is given the shaggy body her name promises.

sentences.t:
et patre Dictaeo, sed matre Laconide nati
Labros et Argiodus, et acutae vocis Hylactor,
sentences.l: and Labros and Argiodus, born of a Dictaean father but a Laconian mother, and Hylactor of the sharp voice,
sentences.i: Labros and Argiodus, sired by a Cretan on a Spartan bitch; Hylactor of the shrill voice;
sentences.n: Dictaeus is 'of Mount Dicte', so Cretan; Laconis is a Greek feminine adjective in -is, 'Spartan woman' — the two prestige breeds crossed. patre and matre are ablatives of origin with nati. acutae vocis is a genitive of description. Labros 'Fierce', Argiodus 'White-tooth', Hylactor 'Barker' — and the barker gets the piercing voice.

sentences.t: quosque referre mora est.
sentences.l: and those whom it is a delay to recount.
sentences.i: and others there is no time to name.
sentences.n: mora est with an infinitive is an idiom, 'it would be a waste of time to'. quos has no expressed antecedent — Latin lets the relative carry 'those' inside itself, and the -que hooks the whole clause onto the string of names: 'and [those] whom it would take too long to recount'. The catalogue ends by refusing to end — the joke is that the list could go on, and the poet breaks it off precisely because the dogs will not wait.

sentences.t:
Ea turba cupidine praedae
per rupes scopulosque adituque carentia saxa,
quaque est difficilis quaque est via nulla, sequuntur.
sentences.l: That crowd, in their lust for the prey, follow over crags and cliffs and rocks that lack any approach, both where the way is hard and where there is no way at all.
sentences.i: That whole pack, wild for the quarry, comes on over crags and cliffs and rocks with no way up them, where the going is hard and where there is no going at all.
sentences.n: turba is grammatically singular but takes a plural verb, sequuntur — construction according to sense, because a crowd is many. careo takes the ablative, so adituque carentia saxa is 'rocks lacking approach'. The repeated quaque… quaque drives the chase forward, and cupidine praedae is an ablative of cause: they are not obeying anyone now.

sentences.t:
Ille fugit per quae fuerat loca saepe secutus,
heu famulos fugit ipse suos.
sentences.l: He flees through the places through which he had often followed — alas, he himself flees his own servants.
sentences.i: He runs through the country he had so often hunted over — himself, alas, running from his own servants.
sentences.n: The relative clause swallows its antecedent again: per quae fuerat loca… secutus is 'through the places through which he had followed'. The same verb fugit stands at both ends of the reversal, once of him hunting and once of him hunted. heu is the narrator's own cry, not Actaeon's. The famuli he flees are the dogs: Ovid gives the pack the word for the slaves of a Roman household, which is also why they are called his dominum, 'master', at 235 and 250.

sentences.t:
Clamare libebat
“Actaeon ego sum, dominum cognoscite vestrum!”
sentences.l: It was pleasing [to him] to shout out, 'I am Actaeon — recognise your own master!'
sentences.i: He longed to shout: 'It is I, Actaeon — know your own master!'
sentences.n: The name at last. Ovid has withheld 'Actaeon' for ninety lines — nepos, Hyantius, Autonoeius heros — and releases it only inside a sentence that cannot be said. libebat is impersonal with an infinitive, 'there was pleasure to him in shouting': it names the wish, not the act, and the next four words cancel it.

sentences.t: Verba animo desunt: resonat latratibus aether.
sentences.l: Words are wanting to his mind: the air rings with barking.
sentences.i: The words fail his mind; the sky rings with baying.
sentences.n: desum takes the dative, animo — and it is the mind, not the voice, that is left standing there without words, which is the point made at 203. The two halves are set side by side with nothing joining them: his silence, their noise. The same verb desunt will return at 237 to measure his body.

sentences.t:
Prima Melanchaetes in tergo vulnera fecit,
proxima Therodamas, Oresitrophus haesit in armo:
sentences.l: Melanchaetes made the first wounds in his back, Therodamas the next; Oresitrophus fastened on his shoulder:
sentences.i: The first wounds were Melanchaetes', in the back; the next Therodamas'; Oresitrophus clung fast to his shoulder:
sentences.n: Three more speaking names, and these are the ones that bite: Melanchaetes 'Black-hair', Therodamas 'Beast-tamer', Oresitrophus 'Mountain-reared'. proxima has fecit understood from the first clause. armus is properly the shoulder of a beast, stretched to men only rarely and in verse — the Latin has stopped treating him as human several words before the dogs have finished.

sentences.t:
tardius exierant, sed per compendia montis
anticipata via est.
sentences.l: they had set out later, but by short cuts over the mountain the way was taken in advance.
sentences.i: they had started later, but by cutting across the mountain the road was already gained.
sentences.n: anticipare is literally 'to take beforehand', and the passive anticipata via est leaves the dogs out of the sentence, as though the short cut did it. compendium is a saving — of money in prose, of distance here. The pluperfect exierant explains, after the fact, why these three arrived first: Ovid gives the tactics of the kill as calmly as a hunting manual.

sentences.t:
Dominum retinentibus illis,
cetera turba coit confertque in corpore dentes.
sentences.l: With those holding their master, the rest of the crowd comes together and drives its teeth into the body.
sentences.i: While those three hold their master fast, the rest of the pack closes in and sinks its teeth into the body.
sentences.n: Another ablative absolute, this time with a present participle: 'with them holding'. Ovid writes dominum, 'their master', not 'him' — the word choice is the horror, since it is still true. confert dentes uses the verb for bringing weapons to bear, and the sentence holds dominum and corpus together in one line, the man's word and the carcass's. Note too that turba here takes singular verbs (coit, confert) where at 227 the same noun took a plural: Latin lets a writer follow the form or the sense, and Ovid takes both within a dozen lines.

sentences.t: Iam loca vulneribus desunt.
sentences.l: Now places are wanting for wounds.
sentences.i: By now there is no room left on him for a wound.
sentences.n: Four words, and the narrative stops dead. desunt is the same verb as at 231, where words failed his mind; here it measures the surface of a body. Latin says it as arithmetic, which is worse than saying it as horror.

sentences.t:
Gemit ille sonumque,
etsi non hominis, quem non tamen edere possit
cervus habet, maestisque replet iuga nota querellis.
sentences.l: He groans, and he has a sound which, though not a man's, yet a stag could not utter, and he fills the familiar ridges with mournful laments.
sentences.i: He groans, and the sound he makes is no man's, and yet no stag could make it either; and he fills the ridges he knows with grieving cries.
sentences.n: possit is a potential subjunctive in the relative clause, 'which a stag would not be able to produce': the sound falls between the two species, exactly as he does. The word order sets sonum first and holds habet back until after both qualifications, so the sound is described before we are told he has it. iuga nota — the ridges he knows, his own hunting ground, still his and no longer his.

sentences.t:
Et genibus pronis supplex similisque roganti
circumfert tacitos tamquam sua bracchia vultus.
sentences.l: And on bent knees, a suppliant and like one entreating, he carries his silent face around, as though it were his arms.
sentences.i: And down on his knees, a suppliant with the look of one pleading, he turns his mute face this way and that in place of the arms he no longer has.
sentences.n: tamquam sua bracchia is the cruellest three words in the tale: the Roman gesture of supplication is made with outstretched arms, and his arms became the long shanks of 196–197. So the face has to do it, and the face cannot speak. genibus pronis is an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'with knees bowed'.

sentences.t:
At comites rapidum solitis hortatibus agmen
ignari instigant oculisque Actaeona quaerunt
et velut absentem certatim Actaeona clamant
sentences.l: But his companions, not knowing, urge on the racing pack with the accustomed shouts, and look for Actaeon with their eyes, and, as though he were absent, cry 'Actaeon!' in rivalry with one another,
sentences.i: But his friends, knowing nothing, cheer the racing pack on with the usual calls, hunt for Actaeon with their eyes, and shout 'Actaeon!' each louder than the last, as though he were somewhere else,
sentences.n: Actaeona is the Greek accusative singular, which Ovid keeps rather than latinising it to Actaeonem — the name is Greek and stays Greek. ignari is dropped in a line late and does all the work: one adjective, and the men cheering the pack on are cheering it onto their own master. The name they are shouting is the one he could not say at 230, and it is shouted twice in two lines.

sentences.t:
(ad nomen caput ille refert), et abesse queruntur
nec capere oblatae segnem spectacula praedae.
sentences.l: (at the name he turns his head round), and they complain that he is away and that, sluggish, he is not taking in the spectacle of the quarry offered.
sentences.i: (at his name he turns his head), and they grumble that he is missing it, too slow to catch the show of the quarry laid on for him.
sentences.n: The parenthesis is the point of the whole passage: the name reaches him, his head comes round, and that is the entire reply he can make — and Ovid puts it in brackets, so the reader sees it while the huntsmen do not. abesse and capere are infinitives of indirect statement after queruntur, with the subject 'him' left unexpressed. oblatae praedae… spectacula, 'the show of the quarry put on offer' — he is the quarry, and the show is being complained about on his behalf.

sentences.t:
Vellet abesse quidem, sed adest; velletque videre,
non etiam sentire canum fera facta suorum.
sentences.l: He would indeed wish to be away, but he is present; and he would wish to see, not also to feel, the savage deeds of his own hounds.
sentences.i: He would indeed wish to be elsewhere — but he is here; and he would wish to watch, not also to feel, the savagery of his own hounds.
sentences.n: vellet is an imperfect subjunctive of unreal wish: 'he would wish, if wishing were any use'. Everything turns on two verbs — videre is what a huntsman does, sentire is what the quarry does — and Latin can put both under one wish, which English can only just manage. suorum lands last in the sentence: his own.

sentences.t:
Undique circumstant mersisque in corpore rostris
dilacerant falsi dominum sub imagine cervi.
sentences.l: On every side they stand round, and with their muzzles sunk in his body they tear their master to pieces under the false shape of a stag.
sentences.i: They ring him round on every side and, muzzles buried in his body, tear their master apart beneath the lying shape of a stag.
sentences.n: mersis in corpore rostris is an ablative absolute. rostrum is the snout of a beast: throughout these lines the dogs get animal vocabulary and their victim keeps human vocabulary (dominum), and the sentence puts both in one line. falsi… cervi is split wide around sub imagine, so that dominum sits physically inside the false stag, which is exactly what has happened.

sentences.t:
nec nisi finita per plurima vulnera vita
ira pharetratae fertur satiata Dianae.
sentences.l: and not until his life was ended through very many wounds is the anger of quivered Diana reported to have been glutted.
sentences.i: and only when his life had been ended through wound after wound, they say, was the wrath of quiver-bearing Diana satisfied.
sentences.n: fertur, 'is said', hands the whole story over to rumour at the last moment — Ovid declines to vouch for the verdict, and the lines that follow this tale in the poem show people arguing about whether Diana went too far. satiata answers satiatae in the tale's opening sentence, where the hounds were 'glutted with their master's blood': the frame closes on the same word, now applied to the goddess. finita… vita is an ablative absolute; pharetrata, 'quiver-bearing', is her cult epithet, and it names the weapon she wished for at 188 and did not need.
